chunks: The hadith of the atheist (zindiq) who came to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and it was from the words of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him):

'Your statement that there are two (gods) cannot be free from the possibility that they are both eternal and powerful, or both weak, or one is powerful and the other weak. If they were both powerful, why does not each one of the two repel its companion and be alone in governance? And if you claim that one is powerful and the other weak, then it is proven that He is One — as we say — due to the manifest incapacity of the second.

If you say they are two, it cannot be free from their being in total agreement from every aspect or in total disagreement from every aspect. When we see creation ordered, the celestial sphere moving, governance unified, and night and day, sun and moon — the soundness of the order and governance, and the harmony of affairs all point to the Regulator being One. Then it would be necessary for you, if you claim two, that there be a gap between them so that they may be two. So that gap itself becomes a third eternal entity alongside them, and three would be required of you. If you claim three, the same would apply as with two, until there is a gap between them, making them five, and then you would end up in the numbering at what has no end in its multitude.'

Hisham said: It was part of the atheist's questioning that he said, 'So what is the proof of Him?' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The existence of effects proves that there is a Maker who made them. Do you not see that when you look at a well-constructed building you know it has a builder, even if you have not seen the builder or witnessed its construction?'

He said, 'So what is He?' He said: 'A thing unlike all things. I return with my words to establishing a meaning: He is a thing in the true reality of thing-ness, except that He has no body, no form, cannot be felt, cannot be touched, and cannot be perceived by the five senses. Imaginations cannot grasp Him, the ages do not diminish Him, and time does not change Him.'

key_terms.التَّدْبِير: Governance, administration — refers to the management and ordering of the universe
key_terms.الشَّيْئِيَّة: Thing-ness, substantiality — a philosophical term affirming God's ontological reality without assimilating Him to created things
key_terms.الْأَفَاعِيل: Effects, actions, works — the plural of fi'l (act); refers to observable phenomena as evidence for their Maker
key_terms.الْحَوَاسّ الْخَمْس: The five senses — sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch; God transcends all of them
key_terms.زِنْدِيق: Zindiq — a term used in classical Islamic sources for a dualist heretic, often associated with Manichaeism; one who professes Islam outwardly while holding heterodox beliefs

ai.seo_question: How did Imam al-Sadiq refute the claim that there are two gods?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) engages in a sophisticated theological debate with an atheist (zindiq), reported by his companion Hisham ibn al-Hakam. The Imam refutes dualism (the claim that two gods exist) through logical arguments about power, governance, and the impossibility of a gap between two eternal beings, then demonstrates God's existence through the cosmological argument (the ordered universe requires a single Regulator), and finally describes God's nature as transcending all categories of created existence — beyond body, form, and sensory perception. This dialogue reflects the vibrant intellectual culture of 2nd-century AH Basra and Kufa, where Shia theologians actively engaged with Manichaean and other dualist currents.
